question: North Carolina law requires motorcycle helmets to comply, effective January 2008, with which federal safety standard?
explanation: North Carolina law requires the operator and all passengers to wear a helmet that complies (effective January 2008) with Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) 218.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: What symbol must be permanently installed by the manufacturer on the back of a compliant safety helmet?
explanation: Compliant safety helmets will have the symbol "DOT" permanently installed by the manufacturer on the back of the helmet.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: According to the handbook, about how many motorcycle crashes result in head or neck injuries?
explanation: One out of every five motorcycle crashes results in head or neck injuries, and these account for a majority of serious and fatal injuries to motorcyclists.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: In a study of more than 900 motorcycle crashes where 40% of riders wore helmets, how many cases were found in which a helmet kept a rider from spotting danger to the side?
explanation: The study did not find even one case in which a helmet kept a rider from spotting danger, refuting the idea that helmets significantly limit peripheral vision.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: According to the handbook, most motorcycle crashes happen:
choice_a: On short trips of less than five miles, just a few minutes after starting out
choice_d: Only after several hours of continuous riding
explanation: Most crashes happen on short trips (less than five miles long), just a few minutes after starting out.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: At the speeds most crashes occur (under 30 mph), an approved helmet can cut the number and severity of head injuries by about:
explanation: Most riders are riding slower than 30 mph when a crash occurs, and at these speeds helmets can cut both the number and severity of head injuries by half.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: No matter what speed a crash occurs at, helmeted riders are how much more likely than unhelmeted riders to survive a head injury?
explanation: No matter what the speed, helmeted riders are three times more likely to survive head injuries than those not wearing helmets at the time of the crash.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6, 'Helmet Use'

question: A label from which organization gives added assurance of helmet quality beyond the required DOT standard?
explanation: A helmet should meet U.S. DOT and state standards; a label from the Snell Memorial Foundation gives you added assurance of quality.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Helmet Selection'

question: Besides the DOT symbol on the back, a compliant helmet must also have a permanently attached interior label showing:
choice_a: The manufacturer's name or identification, model, size, year of manufacture, and shell/liner construction materials
choice_b: The retail price and warranty period
choice_c: The rider's name and driver's license number
choice_d: A barcode linking to the seller's website
explanation: The interior label must have the manufacturer's name or identification, the precise model, size, year of manufacture, and type of shell and liner construction materials, plus cleaning and care instructions.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.6-7, 'Helmet Use'

question: The handbook describes two primary types of helmets providing different levels of coverage. What are they?
explanation: There are two primary types of helmets, providing two different levels of coverage: three-quarter and full face.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Helmet Selection'

question: For maximum protection, a helmet should be free of obvious defects and should:
choice_a: Fit loosely so it can be removed quickly
choice_b: Only cover the top of the head
choice_c: Fit snugly all the way around
choice_d: Be worn without fastening the retention strap for comfort
explanation: Whichever style you choose, get the most protection by making sure the helmet fits snugly all the way around and has no obvious defects such as cracks, loose padding, or frayed straps.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Helmet Selection'

question: A plastic shatter-resistant faceshield helps protect:
choice_c: Nothing that a windshield doesn't already cover
choice_d: Your whole face, including from wind, dust, dirt, rain, insects, and thrown-up pebbles
explanation: A plastic shatter-resistant faceshield can help protect your whole face in a crash, and also protects you from wind, dust, dirt, rain, insects, and pebbles thrown up from vehicles ahead.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Compared to a faceshield, goggles:
choice_a: Protect your eyes but not the rest of your face
choice_b: Protect the whole face equally well
choice_d: Are only effective in cold weather
explanation: Goggles protect your eyes, though they won't protect the rest of your face like a faceshield does.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Can a windshield substitute for a faceshield or goggles?
choice_a: Yes, a windshield alone is sufficient eye protection
choice_b: No -- most windshields will not protect the eyes from wind, and neither will eyeglasses or sunglasses
choice_c: Yes, but only at speeds above 45 mph
choice_d: Only on motorcycles equipped with fairings
explanation: A windshield is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles. Most windshields will not protect your eyes from the wind, and neither will eyeglasses or sunglasses.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: When should tinted eye protection not be worn?
choice_c: At night or any other time when little light is available
explanation: Tinted eye protection should not be worn at night or any other time when little light is available.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.7, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Wearing a jacket even in warm weather helps:
explanation: Wear a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration; many are designed to protect without overheating the rider, even on summer days.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.8, 'Clothing'

question: According to the handbook, which material offers the most protection for a riding jacket and pants?
explanation: Jacket and pants should cover the arms and legs completely; leather offers the most protection, though sturdy synthetic material provides a lot of protection as well.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.8, 'Clothing'

question: Riding boots or shoes should:
choice_b: Be high and sturdy enough to cover and support the ankles, with hard, durable, slip-resistant soles
choice_c: Have long, loose laces for quick removal
choice_d: Have smooth leather soles for style
explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support, with soles of hard, durable, slip-resistant material; laces should be tucked in so they won't catch.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.8, 'Clothing'

question: Riding gloves should be made of:
choice_b: Any material, since gloves don't help in a crash
choice_c: Leather or a similarly durable material
explanation: Gloves allow a better grip and help protect your hands in a crash; they should be made of leather or similar durable material.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.8, 'Clothing'

question: In cold or wet weather, a winter riding jacket should:
choice_a: Be loose-fitting to trap the most air
choice_d: Resist wind and fit snugly at the neck, wrists, and waist
explanation: A winter jacket should resist wind and fit snugly at the neck, wrists, and waist; good-quality rainsuits designed for motorcycle riding resist tearing or ballooning at high speed.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.8, 'Clothing'
